title: How Agencies Streamline Marketing for Franchise Restaurant Clients Using The Right AI Platform
summary: How Agencies Streamline Marketing for Franchise Restaurant Clients Using The Right AI Platform by Logan Welbaum
body_text: Managing marketing for a franchise restaurant brand is nothing like handling a single-location client. You're not just running one ad. You're coordinating campaigns across dozens, sometimes hundreds, of locations. And, each has its own local audience, budget, and team. For agencies, this is where things get complicated fast. Plai is changing how agencies handle this complexity by giving teams a centralized way to manage multi-location campaigns without sacrificing brand consistency or burning out their staff. The Real Challenge with Franchise Restaurant Marketing Ask any agency that works with franchise clients, and they'll tell you the same thing: the hardest part isn't the creative, it's the coordination. Every franchise location technically operates under the same brand umbrella, but ground-level reality looks different. One location is in a college town and runs lunch specials. Another is in a suburban strip mall focused on family dinner deals. A third is near a stadium and needs event-driven promotions. The brand guidelines are the same, but the messaging, targeting, and timing need to flex. When agencies try to manage all of this manually, building separate campaigns location by location, chasing down individual franchisee ad account access, reformatting the same creative over and over, it becomes unsustainable. Hours get eaten up on admin work that should take minutes. Building a Centralized System That Actually Scales The agencies that handle franchise restaurant clients well have one thing in common: they build systems before they take on volume. That means creating a clear structure for how campaigns are organized, how assets are stored, and how locations are onboarded. Instead of treating each location as its own independent project, they treat the franchise as one ecosystem with location-specific variables plugged in. This is where a workspace-based franchise marketing platform becomes essential. When every franchise location lives in its own workspace under a single agency account, switching between clients takes seconds. Reporting is consolidated. Creative libraries are shared. And when the corporate team needs to push a brand-wide promotion, it goes out to every location from one place rather than through fifty separate email threads. Templates Are the Backbone of Multi-Location Efficiency One of the biggest time-savers for agencies managing restaurant franchises is a solid template system. Instead of building every campaign from scratch, agencies create master templates, approved by the franchisor, that franchisees or local managers can customize within set limits. Think of it like a fill-in-the-blank system. The brand colors, logo, and core messaging are locked. The local address, phone number, offer, and radius targeting get swapped in per location. A campaign that used to take a full day to build across twenty locations now takes an hour. Plai's template system is built specifically for this kind of workflow. Franchisee information auto-fills into branded templates, and local teams can launch campaigns in just a few clicks without needing any ad expertise. This matters a lot for restaurant franchises where the local owner is focused on running their kitchen, not running Facebook ads. Giving Franchisees Access Without Losing Control One of the trickiest parts of franchise marketing is the access question. How much do you let individual locations do on their own? Give them too much freedom, and you end up with off-brand creatives, inconsistent messaging, and ad spend going to waste. Give them too little, and every small request becomes a ticket that slows the whole agency down. The agencies that get this right find a middle ground; they give franchisees enough autonomy to handle local promotions and social posting, while keeping brand-critical decisions locked at the HQ or agency level. Franchisees feel empowered. The agency maintains quality control. Everyone wins. This kind of tiered access model is something Plai handles well. Corporate teams set the guardrails, franchisees operate within them, and the agency has visibility into everything without being the bottleneck for every single campaign. Reporting Across Locations Without the Spreadsheet Headache Every agency knows the pain of pulling performance reports for multi-location clients. You're downloading CSVs from Meta, cross-referencing Google data, and manually building a deck that's outdated by the time it lands in the client's inbox. For franchise restaurant clients, this problem multiplies. The franchisor wants to know how the network is performing. Individual franchisees want to know how their location is doing. And the agency needs to be able to show value across the board without spending a full day every month just on reporting. A centralized platform solves this by keeping all campaign data under one roof. Franchisees can log in and see their own numbers. The corporate team gets a network-wide view. And the agency pulls everything it needs in minutes rather than hours. Why Choose Plai for Franchise Restaurant Marketing Agencies managing franchise restaurant clients need a platform that was genuinely built for this kind of work, not a general-purpose ad tool that sort of works if you configure it the right way. Thus, Plai AI is purpose-built for multi-location marketing. It combines ad management across Meta, Google, TikTok, and YouTube with social posting, branded templates, workspace organization, and performance reporting, all under one roof. The franchisee portal means local teams stay independent enough to be useful, but brand-controlled enough that nothing goes off the rails. For agencies, the math is simple: less time on setup and admin means more capacity to take on more clients or go deeper on strategy for existing ones. Plai makes that possible without adding headcount. ‍ Get Started If your agency manages franchise restaurant clients or is looking to, Plai gives you the infrastructure to do it at scale. title: Exercise for mental health: How physical activity boosts emotional well-being
summary: Discover how exercise can improve mental health, ease anxiety and depression, and support emotional well-being. Learn the best exercises for mental health and how to start.
body_text: Exercise and mental health: A natural prescription for emotional well-being At Meru Health, we know that mental health is deeply intertwined with our lifestyle. Just as nutrition fuels the brain and body, physical activity can significantly shape our emotional landscape. In fact, research now confirms that regular exercise is one of the most effective—yet underutilized—tools for managing mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, PTSD, and even ADHD. Let’s explore the profound connection between physical activity and mental well-being, and why moving your body might be a perfect benefit for your mind. Why exercise benefits mental health From mood regulation to stress reduction, the mental health benefits of exercise are vast and well-documented. Numerous meta-analyses (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) have shown that both aerobic and resistance training significantly reduce symptoms of mild to moderate depression and anxiety . But how exactly does this work? How exercise impacts the brain: Boosts endorphins and serotonin: These are the brain’s “feel-good” chemicals, crucial for mood stability and motivation. (8) Lowers cortisol: Regular activity lowers stress hormone levels, which can reduce feelings of overwhelm or agitation. (9) Promotes routine and self-efficacy: Exercise fosters a sense of accomplishment and daily structure, which are protective against depression and anxiety. (10, 11) In fact, according to the data visualized in the Exercise as Medicine peer-reviewed study image below, some forms of movement—like dance and walking/jogging—show outcomes that are better than antidepressant medication or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression. Best types of exercises for mental health Fortunately, there’s no one-size-fits-all. A range of activities have demonstrated mental health benefits: Aerobic Exercise: Running, swimming, cycling, and walking improve heart health and boost mood-regulating neurotransmitters. (12) Yoga and Mindful Movement: Especially effective for PTSD and anxiety disorders, these practices integrate physical movement with mindfulness and breathing, calming the nervous system. (13, 14) Strength Training: Lifting weights or using resistance bands can relieve symptoms of depression and anxiety. (15) And the good news? You don’t have to train like an athlete. According to the World Health Organization, only 150-300 minutes of moderate intensity aerobic physical activity per week (or 21 to 42 minutes/day) reduces risk of multiple health outcomes. (16) Mental health conditions improved by exercise Exercise isn’t just helpful for mood disorders. Its benefits extend across a variety of mental health conditions: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD): Activities like yoga improve sleep and reduce hyperarousal—common PTSD symptoms. (17) Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): Exercise can complement CBT by lowering stress and overall anxiety levels. (18) Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): Aerobic activity can enhance focus and executive function. (19) A powerful, cost-effective complement to therapy While exercise isn’t a cure-all, it’s a powerful, evidence-based adjunct to traditional treatments like therapy and medication. Moreover, in a time where access to mental health care can be limited, exercise stands out as a low-cost, widely accessible intervention. It’s something nearly everyone can begin integrating into their lives today, no prescription required. Meru Health’s takeaway At Meru Health, we know that effective mental healthcare extends beyond therapy sessions. It lives in our daily habits, including how we move. Whether you’re walking your dog, doing a yoga flow, or hitting the gym, each step can be a step toward healing. If you’re new to exercise, start small. Find something you enjoy. And most importantly, be kind to yourself as you build new habits—progress, not perfection, is the goal. Interested in more holistic ways to support your mental health? title: 6 lessons on taste every creative team should take into the AI era
summary: When everyone has the same AI tools, taste becomes the advantage. Six lessons on creative judgment, brand systems and memorable work.
body_text: TL;DR What happens when every creative team has access to the same AI? Leaders from Zoom, Booking.com, Leonardo.AI and Superside share six lessons on the role of taste, collaboration and creative judgment. Producing content has never been easier. Producing great content that people will remember has never been harder. Every marketing team now has access to AI tools that can generate copy, images and video in minutes. The barriers to creation continue to fall, while the volume of content continues to rise. People are truly inundated with content left and right. If AI can create almost anything, what sets brands apart? What can brands do to create memorable scroll-stopping content? That question sat at the center at SHIFT: The Creative AI Summit, where creative leaders from Zoom, Leonardo.AI, Booking.com and Superside explored what happens when every company has access to the same technology. Although the discussion covered everything from brand governance to creative workflows, the conversation kept circling back to the same idea. Taste is becoming one of the few competitive advantages AI can't automate. 1. Taste has never been about aesthetics alone When people talk about taste, it's easy to think about visual style. Beautiful photography. Strong typography. The perfect color palette. Dan Schunk, Head of Creative at Zoom, challenges that definition. "Something beautiful can be created, but if it's not resonating with your goals, if it's not resonating with the overall objective, it just becomes a beautiful picture that doesn't work,” he explained. It's a subtle distinction, but an important one. Creative teams are no longer constrained by their ability to produce options. AI can generate hundreds of them. The harder task is deciding which direction deserves to move forward. Does it communicate the strategy? Does it strengthen the brand? Does it speak to the audience the way you intended? Those decisions remain deeply human. This means that as AI lowers the cost of execution, judgment carries more weight. 2. Develop your taste before your prompting skills While taste is unique to each creative and brand, Kae Neskovic, General Manager of Creative Studios at Superside, argues that a lot of it relies on context and culture. I feel like what taste is, it's actually a really accurate understanding of visual culture and history and knowing what is appropriate and for what purpose. Kae Neskovic General Manager of Creative Studios, Superside That perspective reframes how many teams think about AI. Prompt engineering matters, but prompts don't exist in isolation. They're informed by years of looking at great advertising, understanding photography, studying design systems and recognizing what feels culturally relevant. Dwayne Koh, Head of Creative at Leonardo.AI, described how his team deliberately builds those instincts. “We always get so caught up in these tools. Just look at styling, look at what's new, look at old trends in the sixties. Anchor yourself in taste again before you get into the world itself,” he said. That habit feels particularly relevant today. Many conversations about AI focus on learning new tools. Far fewer focus on developing the creative muscle that makes those tools valuable in the first place. 3. Keep your creative process collaborative Perhaps the most unexpected insight had very little to do with image generation. Jeff Johns, Senior Creative Producer at Booking.com, reflected on how creative work itself has changed. For decades, creative work was something teams could observe. You could glance across the room and see someone refining an edit or working on a complex design. Even if you weren't working on the project yourself, you absorbed techniques, understood who the experts were and learned how different people approached creative problems. The content production itself has never been more of a black box. It's largely hidden. And especially in small creative teams, you used to be able to see somebody on Final Cut or somebody playing with 20 layers on Photoshop, and you could see the work that other people were doing. It gave you a real-time sense check about the skills, the abilities, who the experts are in the team, who is doing what, and how they were doing it. Jeff Johns Senior Creative Producer, Booking.com Years ago, creative teams learned simply by sitting near one another. You could watch how a designer approached a layout or see how an editor solved a difficult problem. Today, much of that thinking happens privately inside prompts, chats and AI workflows. Kae immediately connected that observation to a broader shift. "AI flattens the process. And without process, there is no teamwork," she explained. It's a challenge many organizations are only beginning to recognize. As AI compresses creative workflows, leaders have to become more intentional about sharing knowledge, documenting decisions and helping teams learn from one another. It's really about checking in with your team. If you're working with a core team and everybody has different levels of expertise, different tools that they're mastering it's really important to just speak up, be open, share your struggles, share your learnings, and then you can understand how to pass things off. At the end you get something that is tasteful and relevant for your brand. Jeff Johns Senior Creative Producer, Booking.com 4. Build brand systems that teach people how to think For years, brand guidelines have largely documented visual standards. Logos. Colors. Typography. Photography. When only a handful of people created branded assets, that approach worked well. Today, marketers, sales teams and executives all have the ability to generate content themselves. That changes the role brand systems need to play. Brand guidelines are no longer static documents, but changing and evolving systems. It started to become more of an operating system. The process was more like ‘here are the guidelines, these are the rules of the road, but if you need to create something new, and if you need to expand on this, these are the right ways to approach it’. It wasn't necessarily, like, "Here's the box and this is what you live in, but this is the open field and then as you explore, these are the right ways to be able to do it. Dan Schunk Head of Creative, Zoom Instead of prescribing every possible execution, modern brand guidelines increasingly provide principles that help people make good creative decisions independently. As the document becomes less static, the thinking behind it becomes more important. It's not a PDF. It is a living, breathing document. Dan Schunk Head of Creative, Zoom 5. Treat AI as another creative tool, not the creative process Throughout the conversation, nobody suggested AI should replace creative thinking. Instead, the examples showed AI becoming another tool within an existing workflow. AI is just a tool. It shouldn't be at the forefront... these tools help get you there. Dwayne Koh Head of Creative at Leonardo.AI Dan Schunk shared a similar example from Zoom, where AI helped visualize a television commercial before the team moved into traditional production. His conclusion applies far beyond a single campaign. "Just because you can use it doesn't mean you should always use it." The new challenge for creative leaders is understanding when AI or traditional processes create the most value. 6. Ask one final question before every piece of work How can a creative leader judge creative work in a time when processes, tools and content are changing so rapidly and significantly? Dan Schunk offered perhaps the simplest test. "Would you stand behind it?" It feels like an appropriate question for the AI era. Technology will continue to improve. Models will become more capable. Production will become faster. Those changes make creative judgment more visible, not less. The teams that consistently produce memorable work will still spend time debating ideas, refining concepts, understanding audiences and protecting the standards that define their brands. While AI changes how creative gets made, taste still shapes what deserves to be made in the first place. title: Government contact center: What it is and how to modernize yours
summary: Learn what a government contact center is, how it differs from private-sector models, and what compliant, AI-ready modernization looks like.
body_text: How public-sector agencies are closing the gap between citizen expectations and contact center reality. Most government contact centers weren’t designed to fail. They were designed for voice calls and on-premise systems. That infrastructure has since been stretched to cover omnichannel citizen expectations it was never meant to handle. The agencies modernizing now are doing it because the cost of staying on legacy infrastructure finally exceeded the cost of change, not because they got a new budget. Maintenance contracts compound annually, and compliance gaps widen. Institutional trust erodes with every unresolved call. Key takeaways Government contact centers must balance automation with empathetic human service delivery. Legacy on-premise systems are the single biggest barrier to modernization. Agencies that migrated to cloud platforms gained the flexibility to scale without replacing hardware. AI-powered virtual agents resolve the majority of routine inquiries. The critical factor is the handoff to a live agent with full conversation context preserved. Compliance requirements (FedRAMP, CJIS, HIPAA) eliminate most commercial contact center platforms from government consideration before evaluation even begins. The right platform connects phone, chat, and digital channels in a single agent workspace so agents have the full picture of a citizen’s interaction history. What is a government contact center? A government contact center is a citizen-facing operation where public-sector agencies handle inquiries, requests, and complaints across phone, email, chat, and digital channels. That’s a broader scope than a traditional call center, which typically handles voice alone. Government contact centers manage omnichannel access, enforce strict compliance requirements, and operate under public accountability that private-sector operations simply don’t face. The term “government contact center” covers federal, local government, and state agencies. The scale and complexity vary enormously. A federal benefits agency and a county clerk’s office both qualify, but their infrastructure, staffing, and compliance obligations look nothing alike. How government contact centers differ from private sector contact centers Government contact centers serve a mandatory, involuntary customer base. Citizens don’t choose their agency the way they choose a bank or retailer. That fundamentally changes how you design for both experience and efficiency. The law requires agencies to serve every citizen, regardless of channel, device, or ability. Unlike commercial operations, government contact centers face no competitive pressure, churn risk, or ability to decline service. Compliance requirements shape government platform selection uniquely. Platform evaluation starts with authorization and regulatory fit, before any feature comparison: FedRAMP authorization (required for federal agencies) CJIS compliance (criminal justice data) HIPAA requirements (health-related data) ADA accessibility standards (web-based interfaces) Government compliance requirements eliminate most commercial platforms from consideration before any feature evaluation. Performance metrics are public. Call times, wait times, and resolution rates are subject to Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, congressional oversight, or public reporting. There’s no hiding poor performance when the data is available to anyone. The biggest challenges facing government contact centers today Two blockers prevent most agencies from modernizing: aging technology infrastructure and a widening citizen experience gap as commercial digital services set the benchmark. According to a Gartner survey of 138 government organizations in 2025, 41% cited siloed strategies and 31% cited legacy systems as key challenges to adopting and implementing digital solutions. Legacy on-premise systems and siloed data Most government contact centers still run on decades-old private branch exchange (PBX) infrastructure built before omnichannel was a concept. When those systems were deployed, the goal was to route calls. Nobody built them to unify chat, email, and voice into a coherent view of a citizen’s interaction history. The result is that agents handling a phone call can’t see the email a citizen sent last week or the chat conversation they started an hour ago. Citizens repeat themselves. Agents guess at context. Resolution takes longer than it should. Maintenance costs compound while the ability to add AI, digital channels, or remote capability stays constrained. Citizen expectations shaped by commercial digital experiences Citizens now bring the same expectations to their DMV or benefits agency that they bring to retail and banking apps: quick responses, self-service options that actually work, and the ability to pick up a conversation where they left it. When the experience falls short, it erodes trust in the agency. Low satisfaction scores are a symptom; the deeper cost is institutional credibility. Getting there requires automation for speed and availability, and empathetic human service for complex or emotionally charged interactions. The hard part is threading both consistently, at scale. What modern government contact centers look like Modernized government contact centers share four operational characteristics: cloud-based infrastructure, omnichannel citizen access, AI-assisted live agents, and virtual agents handling routine inquiries autonomously within an AI contact center . All four are proven in real public-sector deployments. The U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) lists 49 different AI use cases for 2025, including AI assistance in handling high volumes of calls, emails, and chat messages, and the Office of the Chief Financial Officer (OCFO) chatbot intended to provide users with quick answers to common questions. The cloud-first infrastructure shift Agencies that migrated to cloud contact center platforms gained the ability to scale capacity, support remote agents, and add AI capabilities without hardware cycles. The U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) plans to implement technology to improve the handling of customer inquiries coming through the National 800 Number. It expects a 40% decrease in average wait times, dropping them from 19 minutes to 12 minutes on average. The SSA’s investment in digital web, mobile, and contact center solutions is essential for improving first-contact resolution. For agencies hoping to achieve similar efficiencies but still running on-premise infrastructure, cloud migration is the prerequisite. Everything else on the modernization roadmap follows from that decision. AI virtual agents for citizen self-service Intelligent virtual agents handle high-volume, routine inquiries: case status checks, hours and location lookups, eligibility questions, and document requirements. Interactive voice response (IVR) systems handle voice-based self-service at scale. Live agents can focus on interactions that genuinely require human judgment, empathy, or authority. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) upgraded the call center solution used for its Women Veterans Call Center in 2025 with the goal of providing “fast, tailored, and reliable support” to veterans accessing that line. The VA also cites cost savings as a goal, noting that cloud contact centers reduce or eliminate infrastructure spend. Some veterans may need more assistance than AI virtual agents can provide. When their call moves from self-service to a live agent, this is what determines success: The agent sees the full prior conversation before the call connects Citizens don’t repeat information they already provided Context transfers seamlessly across the handoff RingCX’s AI Virtual Assistant (AVA) handles citizen self-service across voice and digital channels and transfers to a live agent with full conversation context preserved, so citizens never repeat themselves when escalating. What to look for in a government contact center platform Platform evaluation for a government enterprise contact center starts with compliance, not features. A vendor that can’t clear the compliance screen won’t reach the feature comparison stage. By 2028, Gartner predicts at least 80% of governments will deploy AI agents to automate routine decision-making, which means AI capability is a platform requirement. Compliance and security requirements FedRAMP authorization is table stakes for federal agencies. CJIS compliance matters for law enforcement; HIPAA for health agencies. Verify authorization scope before evaluating features, because authorization for one use case may not cover another. Data residency requirements may restrict which cloud regions a platform can use. Confirm data handling and storage locations before signing. Retrofitting compliance after deployment is expensive and disruptive, and sometimes not achievable without replacing core platform components. ADA accessibility requirements apply to web-based self-service portals. Build accessibility into the platform from day one. Omnichannel and AI capabilities Evaluate platforms on whether they unify voice, chat, email, and digital channels in a single agent workspace. A unified platform means the agent sees every prior interaction—regardless of channel—before responding. Routing without unification still produces the fragmented experience that agents and citizens both hate. The AI capabilities that matter for government contact centers: Intelligent virtual agents for self-service AI IVR for call routing and containment Real-time agent assist to support live conversations Sentiment analysis Interaction analytics Ask whether these capabilities run natively within the platform or require third-party integrations. Each integration point is a compliance surface to manage and a potential failure point. RingCentral’s RingCX is built for public-sector teams handling complex citizen interactions. It’s FedRAMP-authorized, AI-native, and deployable across voice and 20-plus digital channels in a single agent workspace. The case for modernizing your government contact center now The technology exists, and it’s proven in government agencies across the country. The California DMV handled millions of self-service interactions. The GSA chatbot hit 78% satisfaction in its first month. State employees went remote because cloud infrastructure made it possible. Agencies that haven’t modernized carry a compounding liability. Maintenance costs keep rising on systems that can’t support AI or digital channels. Agents can’t see the full context of a citizen’s interaction history. And every unresolved call chips away at institutional trust. Modernization doesn’t happen all at once, but it has to start with the infrastructure question. Cloud-first, compliance-ready, AI-capable. Those three requirements narrow the field to platforms that can actually serve public-sector operations. RingCentral works with government and small business teams building secure, AI-assisted contact centers that deliver better customer experience at scale. FAQs about government contact centers What is the difference between a government call center and a government contact center? A government call center handles voice calls only. A government contact center unifies phone, email, chat, SMS, and social media messaging platforms. It includes self-service options like intelligent virtual agents that resolve routine inquiries. Most modern agencies have adopted the contact center model because voice-only service can’t meet current citizen expectations. What compliance standards apply to government contact centers? Compliance requirements depend on the agency and data handled. Federal agencies need FedRAMP authorization. Law enforcement requires CJIS compliance. Health agencies need HIPAA. All public-facing interfaces must meet ADA accessibility standards under Section 508. Ask vendors for current authorization documentation before procurement. How do AI virtual agents work in government contact centers? AI virtual agents handle routine inquiries like case status checks, eligibility questions, and department routing without human intervention. They use natural language processing to understand intent and respond accurately. When an inquiry exceeds their scope, they escalate to a live agent with full context preserved. Frost & Sullivan reported that 80% of contact center leaders said agent headcount remained steady or increased in 2025, reflecting a blended model in which virtual agents handle routine work and human agents manage higher-value interactions. How do government agencies justify the cost of contact center modernization? The cost justification typically comes from four places: Reduced per-interaction costs when self-service deflects high volumes of routine calls. Lower infrastructure maintenance costs compared to aging on-premise systems. Improved agent productivity when unified platforms replace fragmented multi-system workflows. Risk reduction from compliance gaps that aging systems can’t close. Originally published Jul 01, 2026

title: ARC Prize 2026: ARC-AGI-3 Milestone Prize #1
summary: Celebrating the top three submissions from our first ARC-AGI-3 milestone prize.
body_text: ARC Prize 2026: ARC-AGI-3 Milestone Prize #1 The top three submissions from ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1 ARC-AGI-3 is our first Interactive Reasoning Benchmark. It is a set of novel, video-game-like environments where agents must perceive, explore, plan, and act across long horizons. Due to a hidden hold-out set, these games can't be memorized. They reward on-the-fly learning, efficient exploration, and the ability to set your own goals when the objective isn't clear. Solving them is easy (and even fun) for humans, but remains hard for today's AI. New to ARC Prize 2026, we've introduced two milestone prizes that reward the top mid-competition open-source solutions to ARC-AGI-3. They exist to inspire people to try new ideas and create incentives to push those ideas further. We're excited to award our first $37.5K ARC-AGI-3 milestone prize , which ran through June 30th . Below are the top three submissions from our ARC-AGI-3 Kaggle competition . 1st Place - Tufa Labs, "The Duck" A small open-source LLM that plays ARC-AGI-3 by writing and running Python in a live REPL (similar to the Duke Harness ), treating each game like an interactive coding problem. Notebook · Write-up · Video · Tufa Labs This submission converts the game state into Python variables and interacts with it through a REPL. The process includes reasoning, calling helper functions, running code, taking an action, seeing the results, repeating. It perceives the board through a rendered image, the raw ASCII grid, and a segmentation tool for zooming into regions. It chooses whichever representation fits the moment. To keep playing indefinitely without exhausting the context window, The Duck continuously pops the oldest messages ("infinite play via eviction"), keeping only the system prompt and recent history. The team's stated philosophy is to keep the harness lightweight and generic and let the model drive, and they report the gains came from multimodality and better base models, not hand-built tools. For more on this submission, we encourage you to read the Tufa write-up directly. What's interesting: This submission is the only one of the winners that has the "agent-writes-code" approach. The other two simply use "pick a JSON action." It is a spiritual successor to " Stochastic Goose ," which won the earlier ARC-AGI-3 Agent Preview Competition . Runs Qwen 3.6 27B FP8 locally. Tufa Labs noted that, counterintuitively, hand-crafted tools actually hurt the model; letting it improvise worked better. Featured on Machine Learning Street Talk . The Tufa Labs team on Machine Learning Street Talk 2nd Place - Reki A vision-language model that looks at pictures of the game board and returns one JSON action per step. Notebook At its core this is a "vision-LLM-as-policy" agent: each turn it renders the recent frames as labeled images, feeds them to Gemma-4-31B locally, and asks for a single JSON object describing what changed, a short plan, and the next 1-4 actions. It also keeps a running reflection memory (refreshed every ~10 steps). Additionally, there is a numpy click heuristic mechanism (no GPU needed). Hardcoded rules make fallback and exploratory clicks prefer small, rare-colored, button-like shapes instead of random pixels. A "Dead-signature" notices when clicking a type of object never changes anything and stops wasting clicks on it for the rest of the level. Both are toggle-able via environment variables. What's interesting: Built on the official ARC Prize GPT-OSS-120B template . Reki swapped the model to Gemma-4-31B. Designed for easy ablation: individual features or tricks can be toggled on or off using environment variables, allowing the team to directly measure the impact of each change. Includes JSON self-repair, legal-action constraints, a 1-4 action plan queue, reflection memory. 3rd Place - Md Boktiar Mahbub Murad, "forge" The same "look at the board and return a JSON action" agent as Reki (2nd place), but packaged as a configurable framework. Notebook This submission is similar to Reki's: render frames to images, show them to a locally-served Gemma-4-31B, keep a reflection memory, and return structured JSON actions with repair and legal-action guards. The difference is that this one is wrapped in a profile-driven framework (called "forge") with parameters that control flow. The submission has a generator for multiple candidate actions and an arbiter to score and pick between them and an optional confidence prompt that forces safe/reversible moves when the model is unsure. However, the top-scoring run of thise notebook used a profile that turns off all of the extra machinery. What's interesting: Built on the official ARC Prize GPT-OSS-120B template . Author mentioned that local public-game checks weren't a reliable leaderboard proxy. Congratulations to all three teams, and thank you to everyone who submitted. The second (and final) milestone prize will end September 30th. You can start competing right now. The fastest way in is to copy one of the templates or an existing submission above, make it your own, and see how far you can push it. Head to the ARC-AGI-3 Kaggle competition to get started.

title: The Code of Conduct Steering Our Decisions as We Grow
summary: Running construction projects is complicated. We make it simple.
body_text: Insight Brickanta builds agentic AI for construction, an industry that shapes the places where people live and work for decades. When your technology helps decide what goes into a bid, how a contract is read, or where risk sits in a project, the standard you hold yourself to matters as much as the product you ship. So we wrote down how we act in a code of conduct. It gives us a shared reference for the moments where the right call is not obvious. Why write it down now We are still early. It would be easy to treat ethics as something to formalise later, once there are more people and more process. We think that gets the order wrong. The habits a company forms at fifteen people are the ones it carries at a hundred and fifty. Writing our principles down while the team is small means everyone joins with the same understanding, and the standard does not drift as we scale. The code is short by design. It cannot answer every situation, and it is not meant to. What it gives us is a way to reason: act in accordance with the law and our values, discuss the hard calls with colleagues, and choose the option you would be comfortable explaining openly to family or friends. Where the law is stricter than our code, we follow the law. Where our code is stricter, we follow the code. What it actually covers The code runs across the areas you would expect from a company handling sensitive commercial data in a high-stakes industry. Anti-bribery and fair competition. Conflicts of interest and anti money-laundering. A safe, inclusive workplace, and a clear rejection of child labour and forced labour anywhere our work reaches, including the construction sites our technology serves. Environmental responsibility, in an industry that consumes materials and energy at scale. Two sections carry particular weight for a company like ours. On data, we handle personal and customer information in line with the GDPR: we collect only what we need, keep it no longer than necessary, and never use customer data to train language models or share it between customers. Our information security is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and independently audited. The second is responsible AI. Our products act on behalf of people in a physical industry, so we hold ourselves above what the law alone requires. A human stays in control of consequential decisions. We are transparent about what our AI does and where its limits are. And every finding traces back to its source, the document, the page, the passage, because a risk flag a lawyer cannot check or an estimator cannot price is worth nothing on a real project. The point of a code A code of conduct is only as good as the decisions it shapes. We treat it as a living reference, revisited as we learn and as the company changes. It sits alongside our other policies and our Trust Center, and it belongs to everyone here rather than to a compliance function. We build for society builders. Holding ourselves to a clear standard is part of earning the right to do that work. See our Trust Center for more information about our internal procedures and documents.
